opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most important variables, honestly. Reinforcement learning is only as good as the signal you can give it. If you can reliably tell whether an answer is right or wrong, the model can explore and improve very aggressively. That's why we saw such fast progress in domains like math and competitive programming: you can check the final answer, or run the code against test cases, and the reward is clean.

Where it gets harder is in domains where "good" is fuzzy: writing, open-ended research, advice, long-horizon tasks where the outcome only shows up much later. There, your grader is either a human, which is expensive and noisy, or a learned reward model, which the policy can learn to exploit. You get reward hacking: the model finds what the grader likes rather than what's actually good.

So a lot of the frontier work is really about expanding the set of things we can grade well. That means better verifiers, using models to critique and check other models, breaking fuzzy tasks into pieces that are more checkable, and building environments where the consequences of actions are observable.

There's also an interesting asymmetry. Verifying is often easier than generating. You might not be able to write a great proof, but you can check one. Wherever that gap exists, RL has a lot of room to push capability beyond the quality of the data you started with. So when people ask where RL will work next, I tend to ask where we can build a trustworthy grader, because capability tends to follow that.

r001.rationale: The response says RL has progressed quickly in math and competitive programming because answers or code can be checked, while writing, research, and advice are harder because quality is fuzzy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the most important questions to ask about where RL is going to work and where it isn't. The way I'd put it is that reinforcement learning is only as good as your ability to tell the model whether it did a good job. If you have a clean, reliable signal, the model will climb that hill. And if you don't, it'll climb whatever hill you accidentally gave it, which is usually not the one you wanted.

So the places where we've seen the most dramatic progress are the places where grading is almost free. Math is the obvious one. You have a final answer, you can check it. Competitive programming is similar: you have test cases, the code either passes or it doesn't. Those are domains where you can generate a huge amount of signal very cheaply, and you can trust that signal, and that's a big part of why the reasoning models made such fast progress there first.

The harder question is what happens as you move away from that. If you ask a model to write a good essay, or make a good research plan, or have a good conversation, there isn't a unit test for that. You end up relying on learned reward models or human preferences, and those are noisier and they're exploitable. The model is very good at finding the gap between what the grader rewards and what you actually meant. So a lot of the work in the field right now is really about expanding the frontier of what we can grade well. Can we decompose a fuzzy task into pieces that are verifiable? Can we use the model itself to help evaluate, in a way that's more reliable than the policy it's grading? Can we lean on real-world outcomes, like did the code actually ship and work, instead of a proxy?

My honest view is that the ceiling on RL in a given domain is pretty much set by the quality of the grader in that domain. Where we can grade, I expect progress to be fast and a bit surprising. Where we can't, progress will come more slowly, and it'll come mostly from getting cleverer about evaluation rather than from the RL algorithm itself. That's why I think of evaluation as the actual bottleneck, not compute or data in the usual sense.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts quickly progressing, easily graded domains like math and competitive programming with subjective tasks like essays, research plans, and conversation that lack unit tests and rely on noisier evaluators.

astra-6.text:
I think the ability to grade work is one of the biggest factors in where reinforcement learning can succeed. You need a signal that tells you whether one attempt was better than another. If you have that, you can let the model try different approaches and reinforce the ones that work.

Code and math are particularly useful settings because you can often run a test or check an answer. The model might produce a solution that would be difficult for a person to come up with, but relatively easy to verify. That gap between how hard it is to solve something and how easy it is to check it gives you a lot of room to improve through reinforcement learning.

For more subjective or open-ended work, the challenge becomes defining what good means. You can use human feedback or another model to judge, but then you have to worry about whether you're rewarding real quality or just something that looks good to the grader. So I wouldn't say reinforcement learning is limited to tasks with exact answers. But the reliability of your grading signal really shapes how far you can push it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts code and math, where answers can often be tested or checked, with subjective work, where defining and reliably judging quality is harder.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the ability to grade work is a big part of what determines where reinforcement learning works well. You need a signal that tells you whether one attempt was better than another. In math or coding, you often have a relatively concrete way to check: did you get the right answer, or did the code pass the tests? That makes it possible to explore different approaches and reinforce the ones that succeed.

The interesting thing is that grading can be easier than doing the work yourself. You might not know how to produce a solution, but you can recognize or verify a good one. That opens up a lot of room for learning.

Where it gets harder is when quality is subjective, or when the outcome only becomes clear much later. You can still use reinforcement learning, but the feedback is noisier, and you have to be careful that you're rewarding the thing you actually care about rather than something that just looks good to the grader.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning works well when attempts can be checked objectively, citing math and coding, and explains that subjective quality makes evaluation harder.
